plants.name: Euphorbia pulcherrima
plants.description: In the wild, poinsettia is a tall, sprawling shrub or small tree, nothing like the compact potted plants sold in winter. It can reach 3–4 meters. Its flaming crowns are made of bright bracts, which are modified leaves. They surround tiny yellow-green flower clusters at the center.
plants.bloomingSeason: Wild plants bloom in December, in the dry winter season.
plants.location: Mexico and Central America, where it is native
plants.funFact: The showy 'petals' aren't petals. The true flowers are the tiny cup-shaped clusters, called cyathia, in the middle of the colored bracts.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: This glossy-leaved evergreen shrub flowers in the cool days of late autumn and early winter, when most gardens have gone quiet. Its open, silky blooms have golden stamens at the center. They often drift down in drifts of fallen petals beneath the bush.
plants.bloomingSeason: Autumn into early winter. Flowering usually starts in October or November and continues through December or January.
plants.location: Native to southern Japan. It is widely grown in the mild-winter gardens of the southern United States and Europe.
plants.funFact: Camellia sasanqua is a close relative of the tea plant, Camellia sinensis, and its seeds are pressed to produce a culinary and cosmetic oil.

plants.name: Ceratopetalum gummiferum
plants.description: This Australian native shrub puts on its festive show at the start of summer. Small creamy flowers open, and then their sepals swell and turn a rich red. The bush ends up covered in red, papery 'blossoms' that look like petals.
plants.bloomingSeason: Flowers open from December onwards in southeastern Australia's summer.
plants.location: Eastern Australia, including the New South Wales coast and ranges, and gardens as far south as Canberra
plants.funFact: The red color isn't from petals. After each small flower fades, its calyx enlarges and turns red, which makes the plant a popular Christmas decoration in Australia.
